what: Agents in flight, and why. A finished agent is REMOVED from this file, not marked done — the page shows what is happening now, and history lives in git.

agents.what: Stop a single word in the write-up deleting the AI's top choice
agents.why: The memo demotes any fund whose write-up contains words like monitor, watch or revisit — matched mechanically, after the AI has chosen. Because eight candidates become seven published rows, one such word about the AI's first choice pushes it off the end of the brief. The system we switched on last night can be silently overruled by another model's turn of phrase, on the row that matters most.

agents.what: The cap of eight, worth fourteen points and never examined
agents.why: Between the AI choosing and the founder reading, the list is cut to eight. That cut costs fourteen points of accuracy — the second largest loss in the product — and nobody has ever asked why it is eight. Unlike the cut above it, this one is genuinely expensive to widen, so the answer may be that it is a fair price. Worth knowing which.

agents.what: Widen the shortlist the AI is shown, from eighteen funds to forty
agents.why: The largest single loss in the whole product — nearly thirty points — happens when we cut the list to eighteen before the AI sees it. That number was never a cost or accuracy decision; it was a stopgap for three problems that have all since moved elsewhere. Now that the measuring stick is trustworthy, this can finally be tested properly.

agents.what: The twenty-three points lost before any ranking happens
agents.why: Funds ruled out by their own written rules, rows we are not allowed to offer, and the founder's own screen together remove almost a quarter of right answers before the AI is asked anything. Every one of those founders won a fund we still offer today, so none of it is a closed fund. The question is how much is the world being what it is, and how much is us being stricter than the funders are.
